name: Future Cleantech Architects (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a tonne of greenhouse gas kept out of the air spares people everywhere (heat deaths), so the result is spread by world population; the small European smoke share is left in the world figure.
summary: Future Cleantech Architects (Remscheid and Brussels) does technical analysis and policy advice on clean technologies for hard-to-decarbonise sectors in the EU, with a small sideline of publicly co-funded research on work and learning in manufacturing firms; this model counts the two policies it helped win in 2021-2025, the Renewable Energy Directive's indicative target that 5% of new renewable capacity be innovative technology (2023) and the European Parliament's backing of the low-carbon fuels delegated act (2025), against its spending over those years (€1.37M in 2024). At the defaults a dollar given averts about 0.0012 tonnes of CO₂e, about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, nearly all from the 5% target: the cheaper technology the capacity it causes buys later, anywhere (about half), and that capacity itself where it displaces fossil power (a net cut only in the part the EU emissions trading cap doesn't take back); it is low because the target is loosely defined and voluntary (an eighth of the capacity reported against it is credited to it), Future Cleantech Architects is credited with a tenth of the advocacy, and the next dollar counts 24% of the past average, as it holds about two years of spending in reserve. The result is mostly uncertainty, resting on judgments no study settles (how much capacity the target causes, how much fossil power that displaces, the later learning); the extra cost of the newest technologies is not counted, as no impact analysis gives one, and every branch, the research consortia included, is discounted for missing data.

Renewable electricity capacity the EU adds in 2025-2030
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.eu_new_renewable_capacity_gw_2025_2030): wind and solar outlooks of the industry associations, {{row:ren_new_capacity_gw}} GW (400 to 520).

rows.label: The Renewable Energy Directive's target for innovative technologies, share of new capacity

source.title: Directive (EU) 2023/2413 of 18 October 2023 amending Directive (EU) 2018/2001 (Renewable Energy Directive III), Official Journal L 2023/2413
source.quote: Member States shall set an indicative target for innovative renewable energy technology of at least 5 % of newly installed renewable energy capacity by 2030.

rows.explainer: Adopted in October 2023, from a European Parliament amendment that Future Cleantech Architects says it advised on with others (Annual Report 2025, p. 14: "This 5% target was adopted with support from Future Cleantech Architects and other partners"). Indicative: no penalty if a country misses it.

rows.label: Innovative renewable capacity if every country met the target
rows.explainer: 5% of the capacity added in 2025-2030, about 24 GW. Future Cleantech Architects' own review puts ten member states alone at more than 25 GW (The 5% Opportunity, 2026), above this EU-wide figure because it rests on the national plans' targets, which run ahead of the industry outlooks; the model takes the outlooks (the shared fact, whose high end covers it) as the best guess of what is built.

rows.label: Electricity a gigawatt of innovative renewables makes in a year
rows.explainer: The directive's definition is broad (any technology that "improves, in at least one way, comparable state-of-the-art renewable energy technology", Article 2(14b)): improved solar and wind as much as floating offshore wind, ocean energy or next-generation geothermal. Our judgment, a capacity factor of 30% (15% for improved solar to 50% for a geothermal-heavy mix), times the 8,760 hours of a year.

rows.label: Coal's share of the fossil power displaced (by MWh)
rows.explainer: Gas plants set the margin in most EU hours, coal in some until its phase-out: coal made 269 TWh of EU power in 2024 and gas 430 TWh (Ember, European Electricity Review 2025), so 38% of fossil power, falling by 2030 as countries close their plants. Our judgment, 20% of the displaced fossil power is coal (gas only, 0, to 45% where lignite still runs).

rows.label: CO₂ per MWh of a gas combined-cycle plant

source.title: IPCC (2014), Climate Change 2014: Mitigation, Working Group III, Annex III: Technology-specific cost and performance parameters
source.page: Table A.III.2, gas combined cycle, direct emissions: 350 / 370 / 490 g CO₂eq/kWh (min / median / max)

rows.explainer: Direct emissions of a gas combined-cycle plant, the IPCC's median and range.

rows.label: CO₂ per MWh of a coal plant

source.title: IPCC (2014), Climate Change 2014: Mitigation, Working Group III, Annex III: Technology-specific cost and performance parameters
source.page: Table A.III.2, coal pulverised, direct emissions: 670 / 760 / 870 g CO₂eq/kWh (min / median / max)

rows.explainer: Direct emissions of a hard-coal plant, the IPCC's median and range; lignite, higher (about 1.0-1.1), runs in only a few member states and is not separately counted, a small understatement of the coal end.

rows.label: CO₂ per MWh of the fossil power displaced
rows.explainer: Gas and coal by their shares of the displaced power, about 0.45 tonnes per MWh at the defaults.

rows.label: Share of the innovative capacity's output that displaces fossil power rather than other renewables
rows.explainer: The innovative capacity counts towards the same national renewable targets. The final national plans add up to a renewables share 1.5 points short of the EU's 42.5% (Commission assessment, COM(2025) 274), so where the plans are met, extra innovative capacity mostly replaces solar and wind that would have been built; the industry outlooks fall short of the plans (wind 351 GW by 2030 against a 425 GW goal, WindEurope; solar 718 against 750 GW, SolarPower Europe), so in practice part of it is extra, and firm output (geothermal, ocean) runs when wind and solar don't and gas would. Our judgment, 30% (10% to 60%).

rows.label: Share of a cut in EU power emissions that is a net cut under the emissions trading cap
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.eu_ets_net_reduction_share, {{row:eu_ets_net_share}}, 5% to 60%): EU power plants are under the emissions trading cap, so most allowances the displaced fossil power frees are used elsewhere; only those the Market Stability Reserve cancels, or a cap tightened in response, are a net cut. The target's tonnes come around 2030, late for the reserve.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂ a year the innovative capacity avoids directly, if the target is met
rows.explainer: Capacity × output a year (TWh × 1,000,000 MWh) × CO₂ per MWh of fossil power × the share that displaces fossil power × the share that is a net cut under the EU emissions trading cap. No cost is counted against these tonnes (docs/normalization.md 2.21): the Commission's impact assessment of the directive's revision (SWD(2021) 621, Parts 1 and 2, checked) costs no target for innovative renewable capacity, since the 5% target came later from a Parliament amendment; its section 6.6 assesses sub-targets for hydrogen-based fuels, a different measure. Member states meet the target through their own support schemes, so no regulator's figure exists; the newest technologies cost more per MWh than the solar and wind they replace, so a cost row would lower this branch.

rows.label: 5% target: innovative capacity it causes
rows.explainer: The capacity if met × the share reported as met × the share the target caused (about 2 GW at the defaults); the learning below follows from this added capacity.

rows.label: Cost fall per doubling of capacity built, young energy technologies

source.title: Way, Ives, Mealy & Farmer (2022), Empirically grounded technology forecasts and the energy transition, Joule 6(9)
source.page: Experience curves (Figure 2 and Table S1): solar PV about 20% a doubling, onshore wind and batteries 10%-25%

rows.explainer: Learning rates of solar, wind and batteries cluster around 20% a doubling of cumulative capacity, from 10% to over 25%; the technologies under the target (floating wind, ocean energy, next-generation geothermal) have no long series of their own, so the range is wide.

rows.label: Extra yearly deployment per unit of cost fall (elasticity)
rows.explainer: How much more of a technology is installed in a year when it gets cheaper, percent per percent. Measured demand for home solar panels: a price elasticity of about 0.65 in Connecticut (Gillingham & Tsvetanov 2019, Quantitative Economics); California's rebates moved installations by more, a response to the rebate of about 1.2, several times that as a price elasticity in the short run (Hughes & Podolefsky 2015, Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists). Utility-scale wind and geothermal compete on price in auctions, but grid access, permits and sites also limit them. Our judgment, 1 (0.5 to 3).

rows.label: Growth of these technologies' worldwide capacity from 2030 to the middle of the years counted (about 2040)
rows.explainer: Floating offshore wind, the largest of them, is expected at about 2-7 GW worldwide in 2030 and 56-90 GW in 2040 (outlooks by TGS 4C, Rystad Energy and RenewableUK), about 13-14 times on the central outlooks; ocean energy and next-generation geothermal start smaller and are less certain. Our judgment, 10 times from 2030 to about 2040, the middle of the years a won reform counts after the wait (4 to 20).

rows.label: Extra capacity built later because the technologies got cheaper
rows.explainer: Adding a small capacity to a technology's stock lowers its cost by the learning exponent (−log₂ of one minus the learning rate) times the stock's share added; yearly deployment then grows by the elasticity times that, so over the years the stock grows by a factor G the extra capacity built adds up to the capacity caused × the learning exponent × the elasticity × ln G, whatever the stock's size (about 0.5 GW per GW caused at the defaults).

rows.label: Share of the later capacity built in the EU
rows.explainer: Floating offshore wind, ocean energy and next-generation geothermal are led by European firms and sites, with the US and Asia growing; our judgment, 40% of the later capacity in the EU (20% to 70%), where its tonnes are under the emissions trading cap.

rows.label: Coal's share of the fossil power the later capacity displaces (by MWh)
rows.explainer: Two-fifths of the later capacity is in the EU, where gas sets the margin and coal is mostly closed by the 2040s (say 15% of the displaced power); elsewhere coal made about a third of the world's power in 2024 against gas's fifth (Ember, Global Electricity Review 2025), so over half of fossil power outside the EU, falling by the 2040s. 0.4 × 15% + 0.6 × 55% ≈ 40%. Our judgment, 40% coal (10% to 70%).

rows.label: CO₂ per MWh of the fossil power the later capacity displaces
rows.explainer: Gas and coal by their shares of the power the later capacity displaces.

rows.label: Later tonnes a year from the extra capacity built
rows.formula: learn_gw * ren_twh_per_gw_year * 1e6 * learn_tco2_per_mwh * ren_fossil_displaced_share * (learn_eu_share * eu_ets_net_share + 1 - learn_eu_share)
rows.explainer: The extra later capacity × output × CO₂ per MWh of the fossil power it displaces × the share displacing fossil power, as for the target's own capacity, with the EU part a net cut only in the emissions trading share. The counterfactual and delivered share are already in the capacity caused, so this branch takes only the credit, evidence and missing-data steps.

rows.label: Low-carbon hydrogen made from fossil gas with carbon capture and certified in the EU a year, once in effect
rows.explainer: Hydrogen Europe's Clean Hydrogen Monitor 2025 puts the EU's potential 2030 output from gas with carbon capture ("thermochemical" production) at about 600,000 tonnes a year, of a 2.3 million-tonne clean pipeline only 26% under construction (as reported by Argus, 2025); the EU uses about 8 million tonnes of hydrogen a year, 95% fossil-based (Annual Report 2025, p. 4). Our judgment, 0.6 million tonnes a year once in effect (0.2 to 1.5 million).

rows.label: Extra real emissions a looser methane rule would have let through, per tonne of hydrogen
rows.explainer: The delegated act requires low-carbon hydrogen to emit 70% less than the fossil comparator (94 g CO₂e per MJ), counting methane leaked upstream at a default of 5.32 g CO₂e per MJ of gas (about 1.2% leakage; Transport & Environment's briefing, September 2025, calls even this low). The objections to it sought "greater flexibility on upstream methane emissions accounting" for hydrogen with carbon capture (Argus, 23 October 2025). Making a tonne of hydrogen burns about 165 GJ of gas, so the default adds about 0.9 tonnes of CO₂e a tonne; letting producers claim lower leakage would have cut that on paper and let dirtier supply qualify. Our judgment, 0.3 tonnes of real extra emissions a tonne (0.05 to 1).

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e a year the stricter methane accounting keeps out, once in effect
rows.explainer: Hydrogen certified × the extra emissions per tonne a looser rule would have let through. No compliance cost is counted (docs/normalization.md 2.21): Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2359 (checked) came with no impact assessment and states no cost; its Article 3 asks the Commission to assess alternative pathways by July 2028, so no regulator's figure exists. Nor is the certification delay it avoided: a replacement act would have come within a year or two, before much gas-based hydrogen with capture is running, so the delay would have cost few tonnes.

rows.label: Share of spending on the research consortia on work and learning (AgilOLab, DICoLab)
rows.explainer: The consortia's public grants were €40-50k (AgilOLab, budget year 2024) and €20-30k (DICoLab, from 2025) on the 2026 Lobbyregister entry, and research grants were about 2.8% of 2025 funding (Annual Report 2025, p. 22); AgilOLab began in 2021 (Milestones 2021). Over 2021-2025 that is about 2% of spending, FCA's own staff time on them included (1% to 4%); the solar-cement consortium CemSol is climate work and stays in the climate branches.

rows.label: Research consortia: spending in a typical year of the period
Research consortia: yearly income gains per dollar spent, once they come
rows.explainer: Estimates of the social return to research and development put a dollar of it at many dollars of later output (Jones & Summers 2020, NBER Working Paper 27863); small applied projects on how manufacturing firms organise work and learning, with partners in the Bergisches Land, are less likely to change much. Our judgment, 25 cents a year per dollar (6 to 60 cents) over the years below: about $2 in present value at the defaults, as gains to the firms' workers and owners.

rows.label: Research consortia: years until the gains start
rows.explainer: The projects run three years (DICoLab 2025-2027) and firms adopt their results after; our judgment, 3 years (1 to 6).

rows.label: Research consortia: years the gains last
rows.explainer: Ways of organising work spread and then age as firms and tools change; our judgment, 10 years (5 to 20).

rows.label: Research consortia: later income gains per dollar, discounted
rows.explainer: The yearly gain over its years, after the wait, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Research consortia: income gains in units of value, a typical year
rows.explainer: Income gains to German workers and owners, on the log scale at average consumption (the site's European figure: UK consumption per person on the survey scale), with the consortia's credit, evidence and missing-data steps.

rows.label: Share of each win due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%): the part of a won policy that is the advocates' doing rather than what lawmakers, governments and industry would have done at the same time. Both wins are in, so this is not a chance of winning; Future Cleantech Architects' part of the advocates' work is each branch's attribution row.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Years from the delegated act until its tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The shared figure for rules (facts: climate.years_until_avoided_regulation, 3 years, 1 to 6): the act entered into force in November 2025 and certified volumes build up over the following years.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the delegated act's tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the unit's conversion then discounts the heat deaths from the year the tonne is avoided, so nothing is discounted twice.

rows.label: Present value of the years a won reform counts
Discounted years of impact (delegated act)
Years from the 5% target (late 2023) until its capacity runs in full
rows.explainer: The target's own dates: capacity installed by 2030 (Article 3(1)), mostly from 2025 as countries set their targets, so it runs in full by about 2030, six to seven years after the directive, and partly before; our judgment, 6 years (4.5 to 7).

rows.label: Discounted years of impact (5% target)
Years until the later tonnes from cheaper technology come
rows.explainer: The shared wait for technologies not yet deployed at scale (facts: climate.years_until_avoided_technology, 15 years, 8 to 25).

rows.label: Discounted years of impact (cheaper technology)
5% target: expected tonnes from its own capacity, before adjustments
5% target: expected later tonnes from cheaper technology, before adjustments
Low-carbon fuels act: expected tonnes, before adjustments
Expected tonnes a year of the period, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The wins of 2021-2025, each its tonnes a year × the advocacy share × its discounted years, summed and spread over the period's five years; the research consortia's value enters through the bridge below.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: The tonnes are our own chains from industry outlooks and engineering figures, not a regulator's impact assessment, and the learning branch rests on the general learning-curve literature rather than these technologies; ex-ante estimates of technology policy have often run ahead of what was built. For the consortia, the return is from research on research spending in general, not these projects. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1), applied to every branch.

rows.label: 5% target: share of the capacity reported against it that the target caused
rows.explainer: The definition counts any renewable technology that improves on the state of the art in at least one way, and member states label mature technologies as innovative, so most capacity reported against the target (newer turbines and panels, agrivoltaics, floating offshore wind already in auctions) would have been built anyway; the target is indicative. Our judgment, 12% (4% to 30%) of the reported capacity is there because of it.

rows.label: 5% target: Future Cleantech Architects' share of the advocacy behind it
rows.explainer: The target began as a European Parliament amendment in 2022, backed by the research centres' association EUREC (with which Future Cleantech Architects made four joint recommendations to lawmakers, by its own account, Milestones 2023), Ocean Energy Europe and the geothermal, airborne-wind and solar-thermal associations; Future Cleantech Architects then spent €0.6M-1.0M a year on all its work. Our judgment, 10% of all advocates' resources on this provision (3% to 25%).

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: 5% target: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: 5% target: share of the target member states report as met
rows.explainer: With a definition this loose, meeting the target on paper is easy: Future Cleantech Architects' own review of ten updated national energy and climate plans found seven mentioning it and four saying how they would meet it, and some counting mature options such as large heat pumps or conventional power-to-X as innovative (The 5% Opportunity, 2026). Our judgment, 70% of the target reported as met (40% to 90%); whether that capacity is there because of the target is the counterfactual row's question alone.

rows.label: Low-carbon fuels act: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The objection failed by 373 votes to 180 with 20 abstentions (Agence Europe, 23 October 2025), far from the absolute majority of 361 it needed, and the Commission had already promised a revised method for nuclear and renewable power purchases by the end of 2026. The act would most likely have stood without any advocacy; had it fallen, a replacement would have come within a year or two, perhaps looser on methane. Our judgment, 10% (2% to 30%).

rows.label: Low-carbon fuels act: Future Cleantech Architects' share of the advocacy behind it
rows.explainer: It wrote the in-depth analysis of the method that the Parliament's industry committee asked for and presented it to the committee before the vote (Annual Report 2025, pp. 10-11); the hydrogen industry, environmental groups and member states lobbied on the same vote. Our judgment, 5% (1% to 15%).

rows.label: Low-carbon fuels act: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Research consortia: Future Cleantech Architects' share of the resources behind them
rows.explainer: 1: the spending is Future Cleantech Architects' own and the return is per dollar of anyone's research spending, so its spending × the return is already its share; the partners' own staff time isn't in its cost.

rows.label: Research consortia: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Research consortia: counted less as the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no outcome of the consortia is measured; the return is from research on research spending in general.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no tonne is measured for Future Cleantech Architects' work. The tonnes are our chains for whole policies and its part in them a judgment. Every branch takes it.

rows.label: 5% target: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Learning: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The capacity the target caused already carries its counterfactual and delivered share, so only the credit, evidence and missing-data steps apply.

rows.label: Low-carbon fuels act: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: No delivered share of its own: the volume certified is already the expected one.

rows.label: Share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)

rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply (learning at 1, its counterfactual already in the capacity caused); this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only.

rows.label: Future Cleantech Architects' share of the resources behind the wins (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (ren_downstream * ren_counterfactual_adj * ren_attribution_share_shared + learn_downstream * ren_attribution_share_shared + h2_downstream * h2_counterfactual_adj * h2_attribution_share_shared) / (ren_downstream * ren_counterfactual_adj + learn_downstream + h2_downstream * h2_counterfactual_adj)
rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's tonnes after the counterfactual, for reading only.

rows.label: Share of credit used (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (ren_downstream * ren_counterfactual_adj * ren_attribution_share + learn_downstream * ren_attribution_share + h2_downstream * h2_counterfactual_adj * h2_attribution_share) / (ren_downstream * ren_counterfactual_adj + learn_downstream + h2_downstream * h2_counterfactual_adj)
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of the wins' tonnes delivered (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (ren_downstream * ren_counterfactual_adj * ren_attribution_share * ren_implementation_adj + learn_downstream * ren_attribution_share + h2_downstream * h2_counterfactual_adj * h2_attribution_share) / (ren_downstream * ren_counterfactual_adj * ren_attribution_share + learn_downstream * ren_attribution_share + h2_downstream * h2_counterfactual_adj * h2_attribution_share)
rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply (learning and the delegated act at 1); this is their average, weighted by each branch's tonnes after the counterfactual and credit, for reading only.

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (ren_downstream * ren_total_adj + learn_downstream * learn_total_adj + h2_downstream * h2_total_adj) / (ren_downstream + learn_downstream + h2_downstream)
rows.explainer: The branches' own combined adjustments apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only.

rows.label: Work with no documented win in the period, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Most of its climate work has no decided law to show yet: industrial heat and thermal storage (input to the Commission's planned auction for process heat, a dialogue convened with the energy directorate), cement and steel demand, sustainable aviation fuels, hydrogen priorities (Hydrogen Guardrails), and briefings for the Bundestag and the European Parliament (Annual Reports 2024 and 2025). Its spending is in the cost, so leaving it out would count it as worth nothing; a later win would be counted then. 2024 and 2025 are about two-thirds of the period's real spending and brought one small win, so this pipeline is worth a share of the counted wins: our judgment, 30% of the modelled value (5% to 60%).

rows.label: The research consortia's income gains, in tonnes of CO₂e
rows.formula: rc_uov_per_year / (($deaths_per_tco2e * $climate_heat_share * ((1 - methane_share) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -$climate_heat_death_delay + methane_share * @climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2 * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -@climate.methane_heat_death_delay) * (1 + $side_effect_weight * @climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) * (@death_ages.heat_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.heat_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.heat_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.heat_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74) + ($deaths_per_tco2e * (1 - $climate_heat_share) * air_pollution_weight + extra_deaths_per_tco2e + methane_share * @climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane / (1 + ln(1 + $discount_rate) * @climate.methane_lifetime_years)) * (@death_ages.air_pollution_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74)) * $life_value_multiplier)
rows.explainer: Units of value into tonnes at what a tonne of these is worth on the site's scale (its heat and air-pollution deaths by age, as the conversion counts them), the bridge the other climate-policy models use (docs/normalization.md 2.6).

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per year of the period
rows.formula: (ren_downstream * ren_total_adj + learn_downstream * learn_total_adj + h2_downstream * h2_total_adj) / period_years * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) + tco2e_from_uov
rows.explainer: Each win's expected tonnes × its own adjustments, summed and spread over the period's five years, with the climate work that has no documented win added as a share, plus the research consortia's income gains in tonnes.
